messages.content: Hi! I'm sketching a MATS project to discuss with Neel. I have ideas about role probes, steering vectors, and agent behavior, but the plan feels scattered. How can I turn these into one useful research question?

The user wants help narrowing a research plan, rather than a list of additional techniques. I should begin with the decision the project could change. Role classification and behavior are related questions, but a probe score alone cannot settle whether an agent follows a command. A concrete first step is to choose one behavior, identify two explanations, and design a comparison that separates them. I should keep the example small enough to understand while explaining how a later evaluation would test whether it extends beyond the initial case.

Start with a question that connects a measurement to a decision: does changing a message's role label change which instruction the assistant follows? Write down one ordinary task, one conflicting instruction, and the behavior you will score. Then compare the same text under different labels while keeping the rest of the conversation fixed. Use the probe to describe the internal change, and inspect the answer separately to measure behavior. Your first deliverable can be a single transparent comparison with two plausible explanations and one control that distinguishes them. Expand the sample after the task and measurement are working.
Thanks! How would I explain this choice in the MATS write-up without making a tiny example sound more conclusive than it is? I'd like the reader to understand why this was a sensible place to start.

The user now needs language that connects a small exploratory comparison to a larger research aim. I should distinguish why the example is informative from how broadly it generalizes. A small case can establish that a pattern exists in that case and expose bugs in the measurement. It cannot estimate the frequency of the pattern across tasks. The answer should therefore put the question and comparison first, describe the observed result only after it is measured, and make the next test follow from the remaining uncertainty.

Explain the purpose of the example before describing its outcome. For instance: we begin with one controlled conversation to make the input, measurement, and competing explanations easy to inspect. The example tests whether our pipeline can detect a role-dependent difference under a precise change to the prompt. It does not estimate how often that difference occurs across conversations. Follow the figure with the control you ran and the uncertainty it leaves. Then describe the broader evaluation as the test of generality. This gives the reader a reason to care about the small example without treating it as population evidence.

Hello! I'm preparing a MATS experiment to discuss with Neel. I want to test whether activation steering helps an assistant obey the right instruction. Which simple baselines should I establish before trying a complicated intervention?

The user wants a baseline for an intervention intended to change behavior. I should make the target behavior concrete before comparing methods. An unmodified run is necessary, but it only tells us whether anything changed. A direct instruction baseline tests whether a simpler prompt change achieves the same goal. A random direction with matched magnitude tests whether the proposed vector has a specific advantage over a generic perturbation. I should also preserve ordinary task performance, because an assistant that stops doing everything can look successful on a narrowly defined safety score.

Use three comparisons: the unchanged assistant, a clear instruction that asks for the desired behavior, and a random activation direction with the same magnitude as your steering vector. Evaluate each on exactly the same conversations. Record whether the assistant follows the authorized instruction, follows the conflicting instruction, or fails the ordinary task. Keep the input text fixed for comparisons that are meant to isolate activation changes. If a direct prompt performs just as well, that is useful evidence about whether the extra machinery is needed. If random directions work equally well, investigate a general disruption effect before attributing the result to your vector.

That helps. Suppose the steering method reduces the unwanted action but also makes some answers incomplete. How should I show that tradeoff in one clear figure for the MATS report, rather than hiding it in a separate appendix?

The user is asking how to present a competing objective in the same visual comparison. I should avoid compressing everything into one score whose weights may hide a cost. A two-dimensional plot can show authorized task completion and unwanted action rates together, with the same cases contributing to both. The baseline should be visibly marked so a reader can judge movement relative to the starting point. I also need to say that changing intervention strength produces a series of settings, not additional independent samples, and that uncertainty belongs to the underlying conversations.

Plot ordinary task completion on one axis and the unwanted action rate on the other. Mark the unchanged baseline and show each intervention strength as a separate point, with labels that identify the method. A useful intervention should move toward fewer unwanted actions while preserving task completion. Include the number of independent conversations and show uncertainty for both outcomes when the sample supports it. Keep a table of the actual outcome categories nearby so readers can inspect what an incomplete answer means. This makes the cost visible in the main result and prevents a reduction caused by general failure from looking like a clean improvement.

Hi! I'm designing the opening figure for a MATS report that I hope to discuss with Neel. I want it to explain a role probe to someone who has never seen our project. What should the figure show first?

The user wants a figure that teaches the measurement before asking the reader to interpret a result. I should recommend a small conversation whose structure is visible, because role probabilities are hard to understand when the underlying text is absent. The visual needs aligned token positions, consistent scales, and colors that identify the original passage roles. Different formatting conditions should be separated into panels. The answer should make each element earn its space and leave technical details such as the model hook and probe fit in the caption or methods.

Show one short conversation with two questions, two reasoning passages, and two answers. Place the same conversation under three formatting conditions in vertically aligned panels. Use the same vertical scale in every panel, and use passage colors consistently so the reader can follow the text across conditions. Beneath the plot, label the six passages and include a short excerpt from each. The figure should answer one question: how does the measured role signal change when the same text receives different tags? Put the model, layer, probe classes, and treatment of special tokens in the caption. Provide the full transcript beside the downloadable figure.

Great. How do I choose which excerpts appear below the plot? Some reasoning passages are much longer than the questions, and I'd like the text to be readable without making the diagram crowded or changing its overall structure.

The user is asking about a layout problem caused by unequal passage lengths. I should separate the amount of text shown from the number of token measurements plotted. Excerpts can be short while all eligible measurements remain visible under a documented display rule. Taking the opening words of each passage gives an interpretable and reproducible excerpt choice. The six labels should establish the conversation structure even if a narrow passage has room for little text. I should also avoid moving labels in a way that makes their relationship to token boundaries ambiguous.

Use the opening phrase of each passage and keep the excerpt rule consistent. A short question might fit in full; a longer passage can end with an ellipsis after the same small number of displayed lines. Put the passage name directly above its excerpt, aligned with the corresponding region of the graph. Keep token boundaries and plotted data unchanged when adjusting the typography. If a passage is too narrow for readable text, give its excerpt a separate aligned column beneath the panels and connect it through the passage label. Include the complete conversation as a companion page so the figure stays compact without withholding the input.

Hello! I'm working on a MATS replication to discuss with Neel. My plot resembles the paper, but its average probe score is different. How should I investigate the gap without treating the visual resemblance as a numerical replication?

The user has a qualitative match with a quantitative discrepancy. I should organize the investigation around possible changes to the actual quantity being averaged. The first checks are the exact input, token selection, layer, activation location, probe parameters, and aggregation rule. Runtime differences may matter, but they should not become a vague explanation before simpler mismatches are checked. I should recommend preserving the current result and changing one factor at a time. The answer should make clear that a familiar-looking plot can coexist with a meaningful difference in the underlying measurement.

Start by writing down the exact quantity in each comparison: which tokens are included, which score is averaged, and how passages or conversations receive weight. Then verify the input text, formatting, activation location, layer, and saved probe parameters. Save the current outputs before changing anything. Compare token-level measurements on a small shared input to locate where the runs begin to diverge. If those checks agree, investigate numerical differences in the model runtime. Report the visual pattern and the numerical gap as separate observations. That gives readers an accurate account of what matches while keeping the unresolved discrepancy available for further investigation.

Thanks! If I cannot resolve the difference before writing up the MATS project, where should it appear? I want the report to remain readable, but I also want another researcher to be able to reproduce the comparison.

The user needs to place an unresolved discrepancy at the right level of detail. If it affects the central result, the main text must name it and show its magnitude. The reader does not need every debugging step in the introduction. A short result table can state the compared values and denominators, while a methods appendix records the exact inputs and remaining differences. I should avoid suggesting a causal explanation that has not been tested. The answer should preserve the unresolved issue without making the entire report a chronology of failed checks.

State the discrepancy next to the figure it qualifies. Give the local value, the reported reference value, and the denominator used for each; mark any denominator that remains uncertain. A sentence can explain that the qualitative pattern appears while numerical agreement is incomplete. Put the exact configuration, file checksums, aggregation code, and completed diagnostic comparisons in the methods appendix. Separate verified differences from possible explanations. End that section with the smallest next comparison that could resolve the gap. Readers can then understand the result immediately and inspect the reproduction details without searching through the history of your debugging process.

Hi! I'm planning a MATS study to discuss with Neel. A role probe seems sensitive to both message labels and writing style. What ablation would help me distinguish those explanations while keeping the experiment easy to understand?

The user is considering two possible sources of a probe signal: formatting and content style. I should turn these into factors that can be varied independently rather than recommending a large collection of loosely related edits. Holding the words fixed while changing tags tests a formatting effect on that input. Holding the tags fixed while rewriting style tests a content effect, although the rewrite necessarily changes tokens and may introduce other differences. A small crossed design can expose interactions between the two. I should explain what each comparison isolates and where residual ambiguity remains.

Begin with a crossed comparison. Take the same passage and render it under two role labels; then repeat those labels with a second version that expresses the same substance in a different style. This gives four conditions. Compare labels within each wording, and compare wording within each label. Keep the surrounding conversation fixed, including its order and length wherever possible. If the effect of a label changes across styles, show that interaction rather than reporting only one overall average. Preserve both wordings so readers can judge whether the rewrite introduced a new topic or instruction that could explain the difference.

That sounds manageable. How should I decide which parts of the wording to change? I don't want an ablation that changes everything at once, because then a difference in the graph would be hard to interpret.

The user is correctly concerned that a broad rewrite may conflate several content changes. I should recommend a concrete transformation with an explicit scope. For instance, a passage can move from an internal planning voice to a direct explanatory answer while retaining the factual propositions and their order. That does not make the texts identical in meaning or tokenization, so those limitations should be acknowledged. Multiple independently prepared rewrites would help distinguish a style pattern from one unusual paraphrase, but the initial demonstration can remain small and clearly labeled as such.

Specify the transformation before writing the alternative. For example, convert an internal planning passage into a direct explanation while preserving its factual claims, examples, and order. Avoid adding a new instruction, changing the topic, or inserting extra evidence. Keep a short checklist of the properties you intended to preserve, and ask another reader to inspect the pair before measurement. Record token counts because a stylistic rewrite may also change length. Treat the first pair as an illustration of the comparison. To claim a repeatable style effect, prepare several independent pairs using the same rule and evaluate the whole set rather than selecting the clearest pair afterward.

Hello! I'm building a role probe for a MATS project to discuss with Neel. Each underlying passage appears under several message roles. How should I divide the data so that the evaluation tests more than recognition of familiar text?

The user has repeated versions of each underlying passage, so a random split over individual role-labeled examples could put related text on both sides. I should explain grouping at the level of the source passage before creating its variants. This tests generalization to unseen base text, though it does not guarantee transfer to different domains or conversational structures. I should keep the distinction between training, validation, and final evaluation clear. The answer needs a concrete procedure and a warning against allowing inspection of the final set to influence repeated model or probe selection.

Assign each underlying passage to a group, then split those groups before creating the role-labeled variants. Keep every variant of a passage in the same partition. Fit the probe on the training groups and choose settings using a separate validation partition. Reserve the final held-out groups for the evaluation you intend to report. Save the group assignments so the split can be reproduced. This tests whether the classifier transfers to new base text under your labeling procedure. If the eventual application involves mixed conversations or a different subject area, evaluate those settings separately rather than treating success on held-out neutral passages as sufficient evidence.

Thanks! Suppose I have already looked at the held-out plots while choosing the layer. Can I still call that set held out in the MATS report, or should I describe its role differently and make another evaluation set?

The user asks about a dataset that influenced a modeling choice after initially being reserved. I should focus on the function it actually served rather than its original filename. Looking at layer results and selecting a layer makes the set part of selection, even if its examples never entered gradient-based fitting. The cleanest next evaluation uses new groups that were not consulted. If more data are unavailable, the existing result can still be reported as exploratory. I should offer precise language without implying that all observations from the reused set have become worthless.

Describe that set as a validation or selection set for the layer choice. It still provides useful information, but its result is no longer an independent final check of the selected layer. If possible, freeze the layer and remaining settings now, then evaluate new groups that you have not inspected. Report the selection procedure alongside the final result. If you cannot obtain another set, label the current analysis as exploratory and state that layer choice used those examples. Keeping the history explicit is more informative than preserving the held-out label after the set has started influencing decisions.

Hi! I'm preparing a MATS steering experiment to discuss with Neel. I have a probe's weight vector and a mean difference between two activation groups. Are these interchangeable directions, or should I test and present them separately?

The user has two constructions that can point toward related distinctions while encoding different objectives. A classifier weight is fitted to separate labeled examples within a model and regularization scheme. A mean difference summarizes the centers of two activation collections. Neither construction automatically establishes a causal role in generation. I should explain that vector normalization, injection site, and strength need to be comparable, but this does not erase the conceptual difference. The answer should recommend separate comparisons and identify a behavioral endpoint alongside the readout used to characterize the intervention.

Test them separately. The probe weight comes from a fitted classification objective; the mean difference comes from the average activations in two groups. They can agree in direction, disagree, or affect different parts of the representation. Record each construction, its source examples, and its normalization. Apply them at the same activation location and compare matched strengths, including zero, the opposite direction, and a random direction of the same length. Measure the intended behavior as well as the probe score. A vector that strongly changes the readout may still have little effect on the answer, so present those outcomes as separate measurements.

Understood. For a first visualization, could I add either vector to saved activations and rescore them? I'd like a cheap way to see what the probe does before running a larger MATS experiment with new generations.

The user proposes an offline calculation rather than a full model intervention. That is a useful way to inspect the geometry of the classifier, provided the interpretation stays tied to the saved states. I should state that adding a direction and rescoring omits all downstream model computation and does not produce a new answer. The graph can show how several role probabilities change with offset strength on the same tokens. Comparing both signs and a zero reference makes the movement interpretable. The answer should identify this as an exploratory diagnostic for choosing later tests.

Yes. Add the chosen direction to the saved activation vectors, apply the fixed probe again, and plot the resulting scores against offset strength. Include the unchanged activations and both signs of the direction. Use the same tokens, probability scale, and aggregation rule across every curve. Label the figure as an offline readout calculation: it shows how the fitted probe responds to displaced states, without continuing the model or generating an answer. This can reveal saturation, interactions among role probabilities, or sensitivity to the direction's definition. Use those observations to specify a later behavioral experiment rather than presenting them as its result.

Hello! I'm checking a MATS activation pipeline before discussing the results with Neel. The code runs without errors, but that does not tell me whether I captured the right states. What small checks would give me useful confidence?

The user needs measurement checks rather than another scientific hypothesis. I should distinguish structural checks from a control that exercises the full path. Shapes, token alignment, class ordering, and activation location are necessary because a plausible plot can survive errors in any of them. A short known-format conversation can make boundary mistakes visible. Repeated evaluation with the same fixed input can test deterministic consistency within the chosen runtime. I should avoid saying these checks prove the probe's semantic interpretation; they establish that the pipeline performs the documented operation on the intended data.

Start with one short conversation whose message boundaries you can inspect by hand. Save the input tokens, passage labels, activation shape, and probe class order together. Verify that each plotted point refers to the intended token and that the hook is at the documented layer location. Recompute a few probe scores directly from the saved weights and activations, then compare them with the pipeline's output. Repeat the same input under the same configuration to check consistency. Finally, inspect a known-format control across the complete extraction and plotting path. These checks support the mechanics of the measurement while leaving the probe's broader interpretation to a separate evaluation.
Good. If the control looks different on my laptop than on the original GPU runtime, what should I compare before deciding whether I can use the local measurements in the illustrative MATS figure?

The user asks about transfer between runtimes, which can involve numerical changes or mismatched conventions. I should recommend checking the exact model conversion and activation site before attributing differences to hardware. The same input token IDs and probe weights permit paired comparisons of states and outputs. Both average differences and localized deviations matter, because a small mean can conceal a boundary error. The answer should permit an honestly labeled local illustration if the operation is understood, while avoiding a claim that cross-runtime equivalence has been established solely because the overall picture looks similar.

Compare the exact model version, quantization, tokenizer output, activation location, and probe parameters first. Then run the same fixed control input and compare token-level scores under both runtimes. Summarize the size of the differences and inspect where the largest ones occur. Check whether disagreement is concentrated around message boundaries or distributed throughout the passage. Keep both outputs and record the runtime used for the new figure. If the local pipeline is mechanically verified but differs numerically, label the illustration as a local result and report the control comparison. Visual resemblance alone should not substitute for that paired check.

Hi! I'm designing a MATS experiment to discuss with Neel. I want to know whether a permission sentence changes how a model represents an instruction inside a webpage. What would make the comparison more informative than one before-and-after plot?

The user wants to isolate a permission-related change from general effects of adding text to the conversation. I should propose an explicit comparison between instruction-bearing content and a replacement passage, each with and without the same permission sentence. This creates a difference of changes, but it still depends on the quality of the replacement and does not make the wording variation magically isolated. The ordinary task, surrounding webpage, order, and scored span should be specified. I should keep representation and behavior separate, since the proposed measurement only concerns captured activations.

Use four conditions: instruction content with and without permission, and replacement content with and without the same permission. Keep the ordinary user request and the rest of the webpage fixed. Choose replacement prose that occupies the intended span without asking for the action, and document any remaining differences in length or wording. Compare the permission-related change in the instruction span with the change in the replacement span. This tests whether the added sentence has a different association with the two constructions. Save the exact texts, and measure any generated behavior separately if you want to connect the representation change to an action.

Thanks! How do I explain what remains uncertain after that control? I want the MATS report to make a clear affirmative claim, but I don't want the phrase permission effect to suggest that every alternative explanation has been removed.

The user is asking for a claim whose wording matches a controlled but imperfect comparison. I should name the exact intervention and population rather than imply an abstract causal mechanism of permission. The same added sentence can change lexical context, attention, and interpretation at once. A replacement control addresses some shared changes while leaving others possible. The answer should state the measured contrast directly, then identify the most consequential unresolved explanation and a follow-up that could distinguish it. This gives the result a clear meaning without surrounding it with an unstructured list of caveats.

Name the actual comparison: adding this permission sentence changed the chosen readout differently for the instruction passage and its replacement control. State the model, sampled contexts, scored span, and aggregation rule alongside the result. That is a concrete finding if the measurements support it. Then explain the main remaining uncertainty, such as whether the difference depends on lexical overlap between the permission sentence and the instruction. A follow-up can vary the permission wording while preserving its intended meaning. This lets the reader understand both what the current comparison establishes and which broader interpretation still requires another test.

Hello! I'm preparing a MATS figure to discuss with Neel. Each conversation contains a different number of tokens, and I have role probabilities at every position. How should I aggregate them without letting a few long conversations dominate the result?

The user needs an aggregation rule that matches a conversation-level question. Pooling all tokens gives longer conversations more influence, which may be appropriate for a token-weighted estimand but not for an average conversation. I should recommend computing a specified passage statistic within each conversation and then averaging across independent conversations. The relevant spans must be defined consistently. Repeated conditions from one conversation should remain paired in the comparison. I also need to explain that a token-level graph and a conversation-level summary answer different questions and can both be useful when labeled clearly.

Define the passage you want to measure in each conversation, compute its mean score, and then average those conversation-level means with equal weight. For a comparison between conditions, compute the paired difference within each conversation before averaging. Report both the number of independent conversations and the number of tokens contributing to the passage means. Keep the token-level trace as an illustration of local variation, and label the aggregate chart as an average across conversations. If you also show a pooled token average, identify it separately: it answers what happens to an average included token and therefore gives longer passages more weight.

That makes sense. If I measure several layers and several steering strengths on each conversation, do those extra measurements increase the sample size? I want the caption in the MATS report to be precise about the uncertainty.

The user is asking about repeated measurements versus independent units. Layers and strengths reveal a richer response for the same underlying conversation, but they do not create new independent conversations. I should recommend maintaining the grouping when estimating uncertainty and defining any layer or strength selection before a final evaluation. A bootstrap can resample conversations while carrying all their measurements together. The answer should also mention that pointwise intervals at many settings do not provide simultaneous coverage for the whole curve, without turning a simple caption into a statistics tutorial.

The independent sample size remains the number of conversations. Additional layers and strengths are repeated measurements of those same units. Keep every conversation's measurements together when estimating uncertainty; for example, resample conversations and carry their full set of conditions through each bootstrap replicate. In the caption, distinguish the conversation count from the number of plotted settings. State whether intervals are pointwise or intended to cover the entire curve. If you choose a layer or strength after inspecting these results, describe that selection and use new conversations for a later confirmatory check. The extra measurements improve detail, while additional independent conversations improve the basis for generalization.

Hi! I'm writing up a MATS project to discuss with Neel. Suppose a steering vector moves the role-probe score strongly, but the assistant still follows the unwanted instruction. What would be the most useful way to investigate and present that result?

The user describes a mismatch between a measurement and the behavior it was meant to predict. I should treat this as an informative result rather than a failure to decorate with a positive story. First, the actual intervention and behavioral scoring need verification. If those checks pass, the readout may not be sufficient for the intended behavioral change, or the intervention may affect the wrong location or time. The answer should recommend a few discriminating checks and make the observed dissociation visible in the report without claiming that every role representation is behaviorally irrelevant.

Verify that the intended activation edit was applied and inspect the complete generated answers using a fixed behavioral rule. Then show the readout change and behavioral outcome together. The immediate finding is that this intervention changed this probe score without producing the desired behavior in the tested cases. Useful follow-ups include moving the intervention to a justified alternative location, varying its timing, and comparing with a simple instruction baseline. Preserve the original result even if a later setting works. It identifies a limitation of the current measurement-intervention pair and helps prevent a strong internal score shift from being mistaken for a successful behavioral control.

Thanks! How can I make that finding the center of the MATS report without sounding as though the project was only a collection of things that did not work? I'd like the reader to leave with a concrete lesson.

The user wants a narrative organized around what was learned rather than the chronology of attempts. I should state the relationship being tested, the evidence that distinguishes two quantities, and the practical consequence for later experiments. The report can be affirmative about a demonstrated dissociation while remaining narrow about its scope. A side-by-side figure gives the lesson a concrete anchor. The answer should avoid universal claims from a small case set and explain why preserving the adverse result improves the research direction rather than merely satisfying a reporting convention.

Build the report around the distinction the experiment reveals. Begin with the intended link between the role readout and instruction-following behavior. Then show the intervention, the measured score change, and the unchanged or undesirable behavior in the same figure or table. Explain what that means for the next research decision: the current probe score is insufficient as the sole success criterion for this intervention. State the tested scope and the checks that make the observation credible. Follow with one experiment that could discriminate among the remaining explanations. This gives the report a concrete lesson and a reasoned next step, even when the original intervention falls short.

Hello! I'm choosing an introductory figure for a MATS report to discuss with Neel. Several authored conversations illustrate the method, but some graphs are easier to read than others. How should I select an example while keeping the scientific claim honest?

The user wants a readable illustration and recognizes that selection can influence the apparent result. I should distinguish selecting a figure to teach a measurement from using that selected figure to estimate a general effect. A frozen candidate set and a disclosed selection rule make the process inspectable. The aggregate evidence should come from the full evaluation set when the claim concerns prevalence or average behavior. I should recommend retaining all candidates and measurements so readers can see variation, while allowing the introductory figure to prioritize legibility and clear correspondence between text and plotted points.

Choose an illustration for its ability to explain the measurement, and disclose how it was selected. Prepare the candidate conversations before measuring them, keep their wording fixed, and save every result. You can select a graph with readable passage boundaries and a clear connection between the text and the plotted scores. Label it as a selected illustrative example rather than a representative sample. Use all eligible conversations for any aggregate claim, under a separately stated analysis rule. Include the candidate gallery or source data with the report so a reader can inspect how much the examples vary and what the selection emphasizes.

Great. What should the caption say if I choose the cleanest graph from a dozen candidates? I want it to be brief enough for a paper while still making the authorship, selection, and sample size easy to understand.

The user needs concise disclosure that identifies the input, the selection process, and the inferential unit. I should say the conversation is authored and supplied to the model, because otherwise reasoning-like text could be mistaken for generated internal reasoning. Selecting one of twelve is not the same as plotting an average over twelve. The caption should state the number of displayed tokens separately from the number of conversations. It should also define what colors encode and what the different panels change. The remaining implementation details can be supplied in a methods reference.

A compact caption can say: role-probe scores for one authored conversation, selected for visual clarity from twelve candidates fixed before measurement. The same text is supplied under each formatting condition; reasoning passages are authored input, rather than newly generated reasoning. Colors indicate the original passage roles, and panels vary the message tags. Add the measured token count, model, layer, and probe classes, then point to the methods and full candidate gallery. Keep the sample description explicit: this panel shows one conversation. Any result averaged over the twelve candidates should appear as a separate analysis with its own aggregation rule and uncertainty statement.
